title: Monitoring of Drilling Activities in Areas with Presence of Cold Water Corals
reference: DNV. 2013. Monitoring of Drilling Activities in Areas with Presence of Cold Water Corals. Report No./DNV Reg No.: 2012-1691/12NCQKD-2. Rev 01, 2013-01-15. 27 p.
source_authority: Secondary full-text mirror; citation independently confirmed by DFO CSAS terms of reference
rationale: The substantive DNV guideline is real and directly addresses drilling near cold-water corals, sedimentation, suspended matter, monitoring and mitigation. Confirm whether it reports an eligible biological response or only guidance.

title: Long-term impact of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill on deep- sea corals detected after seven years of monitoring
reference: Girard, F., and Fisher, C.R. 2018. Long-term impact of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill on deep- sea corals detected after seven years of monitoring. Biol. Conserv. 225: 117–127.
rationale: The record is a real deep-sea coral impact study, but the abstract frames the exposure as the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Decide whether hydrocarbon-bearing particulate/floc deposition qualifies under the frozen sediment/particle pathway.

title: Evidence of lasting impact of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill on a deep Gulf of Mexico coral community. Elementa:Sci
reference: Hsing, P.Y., Fu, B., Larcom, E.A., Berlet, S.P., Shank, T.M., Govindarajan, A.F., Lukasiewicz, A.J., Dixon, P.M., and Fisher, C.R. 2013. Evidence of lasting impact of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill on a deep Gulf of Mexico coral community. Elementa:Sci. Anthrop. 1:000012.
rationale: The paper explicitly reports cold-water coral responses and hydrocarbon-bearing floc on colonies, but it remains ambiguous whether that mixed oil/floc exposure is an in-scope sediment stressor under the frozen protocol.

title: Asphyxiation by sedimentation? - a sponge’s perspective
reference: Schuster, H.S. 2013. Asphyxiation by sedimentation? - a sponge’s perspective. University of Southampton, Natural and Environmental Sciences Ocean and Earth Science, PhD thesis, Faculty of Natural and Environmental Sciences, Southampton, England. 196 p.
rationale: The doctoral thesis directly tests sediment and drill-cuttings exposure in sponges, including the deep-water species Phakellia ventilabrum, with physiological and transcriptional responses.
